facts.text: I was in seminary when someone used the term inerrancy with respect to Scripture and it immediately categorized that person as a back woods fundamentalist with no education.

I remember that in seminary the normal response to inerrancy was, “How could anybody believe in the inerrancy of Scripture in this day and age after two hundred years of profound academic analysis and scholarly criticism?”
I was asked to write a commentary for the ICBI event on a document of affirmations and denials in brief form for lay people.
I recommend the book “Explaining Inerrancy, a Commentary” by R.C. Sproul with a forward by Dr. Roger Nicole.
I said that the term inerrancy is a bad word strategically.
I said that the Word of God is true and trustworthy and that it needs to be inerrant to be fully true and trustworthy.
I remember being persuaded by an argument that people choke on inerrancy and might cheat by saying they believe it without really believing it.
I remember that the Dutch had a shibboleth test during World War II involving a seacoast town called Schaveningen.
I remember that the executive council debated how to define the organization as theologians concerned to propagate the concept of inerrancy.
I remember saying that inerrancy must be carefully defined and that it does not mean there are no grammatical crudities in the Bible.
